```minizinc
% Include necessary library for global constraints
include "globals.mzn";

% Define the floors as integers from 1 to 5
set of int: Floors = 1..5;

% Decision variables: floor assignments for each person
var Floors: B; % Baker
var Floors: C; % Cooper
var Floors: F; % Fletcher
var Floors: M; % Miller
var Floors: S; % Smith

% Constraints
constraint
    % All live on different floors
    all_different([B, C, F, M, S]) /\
    
    % Baker does not live on the fifth floor
    B != 5 /\
    
    % Cooper does not live on the first floor
    C != 1 /\
    
    % Fletcher does not live on the first or fifth floor
    F != 1 /\ F != 5 /\
    
    % Miller lives on a higher floor than Cooper
    M > C /\
    
    % Smith does not live on a floor adjacent to Fletcher
    abs(S - F) > 1 /\
    
    % Fletcher does not live on a floor adjacent to Cooper
    abs(F - C) > 1;

% Solve the problem
solve satisfy;

% Output the floors for each person in JSON format
output [
    "{",
    join(",", [
        "\"B\": " ++ show(B),
        "\"C\": " ++ show(C),
        "\"F\": " ++ show(F),
        "\"M\": " ++ show(M),
        "\"S\": " ++ show(S)
```
```minizinc
    ]),
    "}"
];
```

```minizinc
% The problem is to find four item prices (in cents) such that:
% 1) Their sum is 711 cents (i.e., $7.11)
% 2) Their product is also 71100... but since the cashier multiplied the prices in dollars,
%    the product of the prices in dollars is 7.11, so in cents the product is 7.11 * 100^4
%    However, the problem states the product is also 7.11 dollars, so the product of the prices in dollars is 7.11.
%    Since prices are in cents, product in cents^4 = 7.11 * 100^4 = 7.11 * 100000000 = 711000000
%    But this is not correct because the product of cents would be huge.
%    Actually, the problem is a classic puzzle:
%    The sum of the four prices in dollars is 7.11
%    The product of the four prices in dollars is also 7.11
%    So, if prices are in cents: sum = 711
%    product of prices in cents = 7.11 * 100^4 = 7.11 * 100000000 = 711000000
%    So product of prices in cents = 711000000
%
% We will search for four integers prices in [1..711] such that:
% sum(prices) = 711
% product(prices) = 711000000
%
% To avoid overflow, we use int64 (default in MiniZinc is int, but we assume 64-bit)
%
% We will use symmetry breaking: prices[1] <= prices[2] <= prices[3] <= prices[4]

include "globals.mzn";

int: total_sum = 711;
int: total_product = 711000000;

array[1..4] of var 1..total_sum: prices;

constraint
    forall(i in 1..3) (
        prices[i] <= prices[i+1]
    );

constraint
    sum(prices) == total_sum;

constraint
    % product constraint: product of prices = total_product
    % Use global constraint for product
    product(prices) == total_product;

solve satisfy;

output [
    "{",
    "\"prices\": [" ++ join(", ", [show(prices[i]) | i in 1..4]) ++ "]",
```
```minizinc
    "}"
];
```

019: Magic Squares and Sequences

An order \( n \) magic square is a \( n \) by \( n \) matrix containing the numbers 1 to \( n^2 \), with each row,
column, and main diagonal equal to the same sum. As well as finding magic squares, we are interested in the number
of a given size that exist. There are several interesting variations. For example, we may insist on certain values
in certain squares (like in quasigroup completion) and ask if the magic square can be completed. In a heterosquare,
each row, column, and diagonal sums to a different value. In an anti-magic square, the row, column, and diagonal
sums form a sequence of consecutive integers.

A magic sequence of length \( n \) is a sequence of integers \( x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1} \) between 0 and \( n-1 \),
such that for all \( i \) in 0 to \( n-1 \), the number \( i \) occurs exactly \( x_i \) times in the sequence.

\( n \)-queens problem is to find a set of \( n \) locations on a chessboard, no two of which are on the same row,
column or diagonal.

A simple arithmetical observation may be helpful in understanding models. Suppose a queen is represented by an ordered
pair \((\alpha, \beta)\), the value \(\alpha\) represents the queen’s column, and \(\beta\) its row on the chessboard.
Then two queens do not attack each other iff they have different values of all of \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\alpha - \beta\),
and \(\alpha + \beta\). It may not be intuitively obvious that chessboard diagonals correspond to sums and differences,
but consider moving one square along the two orthogonal diagonals: in one direction the sum of the coordinates does not
change, while in the other direction the difference does not change. (We do not suggest that pairs \((\alpha, \beta)\)
is a good representation for solving.)

The problem has inherent symmetry. That is, for any solution we obtain another solution by any of the 8 symmetries of
the chessboard (including the identity) obtained by combinations of rotations by 90 degrees and reflections.

076: Costas Array

A Costas array is a pattern of \( n \) marks on an \( n \times n \) grid, one mark per row and one per column, in which the
\( n \cdot (n-1)/2 \) vectors between the marks are all different.

Such patterns are important as they provide a template for generating radar and sonar signals with ideal ambiguity
functions.

A model for Costas Array Problem (CAP) is to define an array of variables \( X_1, \ldots, X_n \) which form a permutation.
For each length \( l \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\} \), we add \( n-l \) more variables \( X_{l1}, \ldots, X_{ln-1} \), whereby each of
these variables is assigned the difference of \( X_i - X_{i+l} \) for \( i \in \{1, \ldots, n-l\} \). These additional variables
form a difference triangle.

Each line of this difference triangle must not contain any value twice. That is, the CAP is simply a collection of
all-different constraints on \( X_1, \ldots, X_n \) and \( X_{l1}, \ldots, X_{ln-l} \) for all \( l \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\} \).

084: 2cc Hadamard Matrix Legendre Pairs

For every odd positive integer \( \ell \) (and \( m = \frac{\ell - 1}{2} \)) we define the 2cc Hadamard matrix Legendre pairs CSP using the \{V, D, C\} format (Variables, Domains, Constraints) as follows:

- \( V = \{a_1, \ldots, a_\ell, b_1, \ldots, b_\ell\} \), a set of \( 2 \cdot \ell \) variables
- \( D = \{D_{a_1}, \ldots, D_{a_\ell}, D_{b_1}, \ldots, D_{b_\ell}\} \), a set of \( 2 \cdot \ell \) domains, all of them equal to \{-1, +1\}
- \( C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_m, c_{m+1}, c_{m+2}\} \), a set of \( m+2 \) constraints (\( m \) quadratic constraints and 2 linear constraints)

The \( m \) quadratic constraints are given by:
\[ c_s := \text{PAF}(A, s) + \text{PAF}(B, s) = -2, \forall s = 1, \ldots, m \]
where PAF denotes the periodic autocorrelation function: (\(i + s\) is taken mod \( \ell \) when it exceeds \( \ell \))
\[ A = [a_1, \ldots, a_\ell], \, \text{PAF}(A, s) = \sum_{i=1}^\ell a_i a_{i+s} \]
\[ B = [b_1, \ldots, b_\ell], \, \text{PAF}(B, s) = \sum_{i=1}^\ell b_i b_{i+s} \]

The 2 linear constraints are given by:
\[ c_{m+1} := a_1 + \ldots + a_\ell = 1 \]
\[ c_{m+2} := b_1 + \ldots + b_\ell = 1 \]

The 2cc Hadamard matrix Legendre pairs CSP for all odd \( \ell = 3, \ldots, 99 \) are given in http://www.cargo.wlu.ca/CSP_2cc_Hadamard/ (and in the data section). There are 49 CSPs. All of them are known to have solutions.

It is conjectured that the 2cc Hadamard matrix Legendre pairs CSP has solutions, for every odd \( \ell \), and this is linked to the famous Hadamard conjecture [Kotsireas].

```minizinc
% Problem:
% Given integers n > 0 and m >= 0,
% find a non-empty finite series S = (s0, s1, ..., sn, sn+1)
% such that:
% 1) For each i in 0..n, si is the number of occurrences of i in S.

% m = 5
%

include "globals.mzn";

int: n = 27;
int: m = 5;

% The series S has length n+2: indices 0..n+1
array[0..n+1] of var 0..sum(0..n+1)(m) : s;

% The length of S is sum of all s[i]
var 1..sum(0..n+1)(m) : length_S = sum(i in 0..n+1)(s[i]);

% Constraint 1:
% For each i in 0..n, s[i] equals the number of occurrences of i in S.
% The number of occurrences of i in S is s[i].
% So s[i] = count of i in s.
%

%
% For each i in 0..n:
% s[i] = number of j in 0..n+1 such that s[j] = i

constraint

    s[i] = sum(j in 0..n+1)(bool2int(s[j] = i))
  );

% Constraint 2:
% s[n+1] = m
constraint s[n+1] = m;

% Non-empty series: length_S >= 1
constraint length_S >= 1;

solve satisfy;

output [
  "{",
  "\"s\": [" ++ join(", ", [show(s[i]) | i in 0..n+1]) ++ "]",
  "}"
];
```

```minizinc
    % ECHO
    [letter_index("E"), letter_index("C"), letter_index("H"), letter_index("O")],
    % OVAL
    [letter_index("O"), letter_index("V"), letter_index("A"), letter_index("L")],
    % GIRD
    [letter_index("G"), letter_index("I"), letter_index("R"), letter_index("D")],
    % SMUG
    [letter_index("S"), letter_index("M"), letter_index("U"), letter_index("G")],
    % JUMP
    [letter_index("J"), letter_index("U"), letter_index("M"), letter_index("P")],
    % TORN
    [letter_index("T"), letter_index("O"), letter_index("R"), letter_index("N")],
    % LUCK
```

```minizinc
% We have three players: X, Y, Z
% and three nationalities: American, English, French
% Each player is assigned a nationality represented by an integer 0,1,2
% The same integer value denotes the matching between the person and their nationality

% We will assign:
% 0,1,2 to the nationalities and players in some order
% The variables x,y,z represent the nationality of players X,Y,Z respectively
% The variables american, english, french represent the player who is American, English, French respectively

include "globals.mzn";

% Domains for players and nationalities
set of int: Players = 0..2;
set of int: Nationalities = 0..2;

% Decision variables
var Nationalities: x; % nationality of player X
var Nationalities: y; % nationality of player Y
var Nationalities: z; % nationality of player Z

var Players: american; % player who is American
var Players: english;  % player who is English
var Players: french;   % player who is French

% All players have different nationalities
constraint all_different([x,y,z]);

% All nationalities correspond to different players
constraint all_different([american, english, french]);

% Link nationality variables with player variables
% For each nationality variable, the player variable is the index of the player with that nationality
% So if x == 0 (say American), then american == 0 (player X)
% We can enforce this by:
constraint (x == 0) <-> (american == 0);
constraint (y == 0) <-> (american == 1);
constraint (z == 0) <-> (american == 2);

constraint (x == 1) <-> (english == 0);
constraint (y == 1) <-> (english == 1);
constraint (z == 1) <-> (english == 2);

constraint (x == 2) <-> (french == 0);
constraint (y == 2) <-> (french == 1);
constraint (z == 2) <-> (french == 2);

% The seating is around a circular table: X->Y->Z->X (passing cards to the right)
% Y passed three hearts to the American
% So the player to the right of Y is Z (since order is X,Y,Z around table)
% So Y passed cards to Z
% The cards Y passed to Z are three hearts
% So Z is American
constraint american == 2; % Z is American

% X passed the queen of spades and two diamonds to the person who passed their cards to the Frenchwoman
% The person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman is the player to the left of the Frenchwoman
% Since passing is to the right, the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman is the player to the left of the Frenchwoman
% The order is X->Y->Z->X, so left of a player is the player who receives cards from them
% So if Frenchwoman is player F, then the person who passed cards to her is the player to her left:
% If french == 0 (X), then the person who passed cards to her is Z (2)
% If french == 1 (Y), then the person who passed cards to her is X (0)
% If french == 2 (Z), then the person who passed cards to her is Y (1)

% X passed queen of spades and two diamonds to that person
% So X passed cards to the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman
% Passing is to the right, so X passes cards to Y
% So Y is the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman
% So Y is the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman

% So the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman is Y
% From above, the person who passed cards to the Frenchwoman is:
% if french == 0 then person is Z (2)
% if french == 1 then person is X (0)
% if french == 2 then person is Y (1)

% So Y == person who passed cards to Frenchwoman
% So Y == 0 if french == 1
% Y == 1 if french == 2
% Y == 2 if french == 0

constraint
  (french == 0 /\ y == 2) \/
  (french == 1 /\ y == 0) \/
  (french == 2 /\ y == 1);

solve satisfy;

output [
    "{",
    join(",", [
        "\"x\": " ++ show(x),
        "\"y\": " ++ show(y),
        "\"z\": " ++ show(z),
        "\"american\": " ++ show(american),
        "\"english\": " ++ show(english),
        "\"french\": " ++ show(french)
    ]),
    "}"
];
```

```minizinc
% Input data
int: num_crew = 20;
int: num_flights = 10;

array[1..num_crew, 1..5] of int: attributes = [
    % steward, hostess, french, spanish, german
    1, 0, 0, 0, 1,  % Tom     = 1
    1, 0, 0, 0, 0,  % David   = 2
    1, 0, 0, 0, 1,  % Jeremy  = 3
    1, 0, 0, 0, 0,  % Ron     = 4
    1, 0, 0, 1, 0,  % Joe     = 5
    1, 0, 1, 1, 0,  % Bill    = 6
    1, 0, 0, 1, 0,  % Fred    = 7
    1, 0, 0, 0, 0,  % Bob     = 8
    1, 0, 0, 1, 1,  % Mario   = 9
    1, 0, 0, 0, 0,  % Ed      = 10
    0, 1, 0, 0, 0,  % Carol   = 11
    0, 1, 0, 0, 0,  % Janet   = 12
    0, 1, 0, 0, 0,  % Tracy   = 13
    0, 1, 0, 1, 1,  % Marilyn = 14
    0, 1, 0, 0, 0,  % Carolyn = 15
    0, 1, 0, 0, 0,  % Cathy   = 16
    0, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Inez    = 17
    0, 1, 1, 0, 0,  % Jean    = 18
    0, 1, 0, 1, 1,  % Heather = 19
    0, 1, 1, 0, 0   % Juliet  = 20
];

array[1..num_flights, 1..6] of int: required_crew = [
    % staff, stewards, hostesses, french, spanish, german
    4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 1
    5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 2
    5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 3
    6, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 4
    7, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 5
    4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 6
    5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 7
    6, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 8
    6, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1,  % Flight 9
    7, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1   % Flight 10
];

% Decision variables
% crew[p,f] = 1 if person p is assigned to flight f, else 0
array[1..num_crew, 1..num_flights] of var 0..1: crew;

% Constraints

% 1) Each flight must have the required number of total crew
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f]) = required_crew[f,1]
  );

% 2) Each flight must have the required number of stewards
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,1]) = required_crew[f,2]
  );

% 3) Each flight must have the required number of hostesses
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,2]) = required_crew[f,3]
  );

% 4) Each flight must have the required number of French speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,3]) >= required_crew[f,4]
  );

% 5) Each flight must have the required number of Spanish speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,4]) >= required_crew[f,5]
  );

% 6) Each flight must have the required number of German speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,5]) >= required_crew[f,6]
  );

% 7) After attending a flight, each crew member must have two flights off
% This means if crew member p attends flight f, then crew member p cannot attend flights f+1 and f+2
constraint
  forall(p in 1..num_crew, f in 1..num_flights) (
    if f <= num_flights - 2 then
      crew[p,f] + crew[p,f+1] + crew[p,f+2] <= 1
    else if f = num_flights - 1 then
      crew[p,f] + crew[p,f+1] <= 1
    else
      true
    endif
  );

solve satisfy;

output [
  "{",
  "\"crew\": [",
  join(",\n", [
    "[" ++ join(",", [show(crew[p,f]) | f in 1..num_flights]) ++ "]"
    | p in 1..num_crew
  ]),
  "]",
  "}"
];
```

```minizinc
    7, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1   % Flight 10
];

array[1..num_crew, 1..num_flights] of var 0..1: crew;

% Constraints

constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f]) = required_crew[f,1]
  );

% 2) Each flight must have the required number of stewards
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,1]) = required_crew[f,2]
  );

% 3) Each flight must have the required number of hostesses
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,2]) = required_crew[f,3]
  );

% 4) Each flight must have the required number of French speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,3]) >= required_crew[f,4]
  );

% 5) Each flight must have the required number of Spanish speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,4]) >= required_crew[f,5]
  );

% 6) Each flight must have the required number of German speakers
constraint
  forall(f in 1..num_flights) (
    sum(p in 1..num_crew)(crew[p,f] * attributes[p,5]) >= required_crew[f,6]
  );

% This means if crew member p attends flight f, then crew member p cannot attend flights f+1 and f+2

    else if f = num_flights - 1 then
      crew[p,f] + crew[p,f+1] <= 1
    else
      true
    endif
  );

output [

  "\"crew\": [",
  join(",\n", [
    "[" ++ join(",", [show(crew[p,f]) | f in 1..num_flights]) ++ "]"
    | p in 1..num_crew
  ]),
  "]",
  "}"
];
```
